faqs.q: What is the typical hourly rate for a forensic scientist in Australia?
faqs.a: Forensic scientists are usually covered by the Health Professionals and Support Services Award [MA000027]. Minimum hourly rates vary by classification and experience. For the latest rates, refer to the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides or use our [pay guides](/blog) page. As a benchmark, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for full-time employees, but forensic scientists typically earn above this under their award.

faqs.q: How do I convert my forensic scientist salary from hourly to annual?
faqs.a: To convert an hourly rate to an annual salary, multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. For example, an hourly rate of $35 gives an annual gross of $35 × 38 × 52 = $69,160. Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool can do this automatically.

faqs.q: Does the forensic scientist salary include superannuation?
faqs.a: No, superannuation is paid on top of your base salary. The Super Guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary earnings (as of 2026–27), up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For example, if your annual gross salary is $80,000, your employer must contribute an additional $9,600 to your super fund. This is not included in your take-home pay. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more details.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Forensic Scientist Salary Landscape

When evaluating a **forensic scientist salary**, it’s essential to distinguish between hourly rates, annual packages, and the additional benefits like superannuation. Forensic scientists in Australia are typically employed under the Health Professionals and Support Services Award [MA000027], which sets minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. The Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database provides the official data, while the Fair Work Ombudsman offers pay guides that summarise the most common rates.

This guide explains how to convert your hourly rate to an annual figure, what taxes and superannuation to expect, and how to use our tools to get a clear picture of your earnings.

### Converting Hourly to Annual Pay

The standard conversion for a full-time employee working 38 hours per week is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks**

For example, if your forensic scientist salary is $40 per hour, your annual gross would be $40 × 38 × 52 = $79,040. If you work part-time or casual hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. Casual employees also receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate, as per the National Minimum Wage ($33.05 per hour casual from 1 July 2026).

Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading. It then calculates the annual, monthly, fortnightly, and weekly amounts. Remember, this assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

### The Role of Awards and Minimum Rates

Forensic scientists are generally covered by the Health Professionals and Support Services Award. The minimum rates for this award are updated annually following the Fair Work Commission’s Wage Review. For 2026, the data is available in the Modern Awards Pay Database. The award includes classifications for different experience levels, and you may be entitled to allowances for specific tasks or qualifications.

If you are not covered by an award, your minimum pay is the National Minimum Wage: $26.44 per hour for full-time employees, or $33.05 per hour for casuals (including the 25% loading). Always check your employment contract and the applicable award using the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay Calculator.

For a broader perspective, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports Average Weekly Earnings for full-time adults at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). This is a useful benchmark, but your actual forensic scientist salary may differ based on your role, location, and experience.

### Tax and Superannuation Considerations

Your take-home pay is your gross annual salary minus tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000
- 30% on income between $45,001 and $135,000
- 37% on income between $135,001 and $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (single reduction thresholds for 2025–26 apply here). Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool estimates your net income after these deductions.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. The Super Guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For example, if your annual gross is $80,000, your employer adds $9,600 to your super fund. This is not part of your take-home pay but is a valuable long-term benefit. Learn more on our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page.

### Using Our Tools

To get a personalised estimate of your forensic scientist salary, start with [the timesheet](/) where you can enter your base hourly rate. Check the box for casual loading if applicable. Then use our [reference tables](/data) to compare your rate against award minimums and industry averages.

Remember, the figures here are estimates. Always consult your employer, the Fair Work Ombudsman, or a qualified accountant for precise advice. The disclaimer below applies to all calculations on this site.

---

*Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.*
